blocks.text: Unlike Burkitt lymphoma cells, which typically express surface immunoglobulins, the lymphoblasts in ALL L3 subtype do not express surface immunoglobulins. Instead, they express other markers, such as CD10 and CD19.
ALL-L3 is similar to Burkitt’s lymphoma.
The image below shows the FAB types of ALL.
Presence of lymphoblasts with vacuoles and cytoplasmic blebs ( Option A): The presence of lymphoblasts with vacuoles and cytoplasmic blebs is a characteristic feature of L3 subtype ALL.

items.text: Association with Epstein-Barr virus ( Option C): Burkitt lymphoma is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) infection. However, while EBV infection may be present in some ALL cases, it is not a defining characteristic of the ALL L3 subtype.

t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome ( Option D): The Philadelphia chromosome, resulting from the translocation t(9;22), is associated with a different subtype of ALL (Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL, or Ph+ ALL) rather than the L3 subtype. Ph+ ALL is characterised by the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (190 kDa fusion protein).

blocks.text: t(15;17) translocation is not associated with ALL; rather, it is seen in acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML), a type of acute myeloid leukaemia, where t(15;17) translocation leads to the formation of a PML-RARα fusion protein (Option D).
Genetic abnormalities associated with ALL: B-cell ALL with recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities:

items.text: t(12;21): ETV6-RUNX1 (25% of the cases) (Option B ruled out).
t(9;22): BCR-ABL1 (Option A ruled out). It produces a 190 kDa fusion protein.
B-cell ALL t(1;19): TCF3-PBX1. (Option C ruled out).

blocks.text: BCR-ABL1 like ALL (provisional entity in 2018 WHO). iAMP 21 ALL. T-cell ALL: NOTCH1 mutations are most common (50-70% of the cases).
CD10 and Cytoplasmic immunoglobulins (Cy Ig) are negative in early pre-B acute leukaemia but become positive in pre-B ALL.

This patient's history of sudden onset symptoms with pancytopenia, high prothrombin time, and Auer-rods on blood smear suggests disseminated intravascular coagulation secondary to acute promyelocytic leukaemia associated with t(15:17) translocation. M3 AML/ Acute promyelocytic leukemia: Genetics: t(15:17) translocation causes PML-RARA (retinoic acid receptor alpha) fusion protein formation. Blocks promyelocyte → myelocyte maturation.

Diagnosis of choice: FISH Smear findings: Increased promyelocytes. Auer Rods: Fused granules in promyelocytes Faggot Cells: Auer rods with a crisscross pattern. Laboratory: Low hemoglobin and platelets. > 20% blasts on peripheral and bone marrow smear Stain: PAS + CD markers: CD 13, 33 + Complication: Disseminated intravascular coagulation therefore, chemotherapy is not recommended.
Treatment: ATRA (All-trans-retinoic-acid) + As 2 O 3 (arsenic trioxide) Best prognosis among all AML.

items.text: t(12:21) translocation (Option A) is seen in ALL and has a good prognosis. They are negative for auer rods.

t(9:22) translocation (Option C): Philadelphia chromosome associated with CML and ALL (worse prognosis). CML: t(9;22) results in a BCR-ABL fusion protein of 210 kDa. ALL: t(9;22) results in a BCR-ABL fusion protein of 190 kDa. Presents with massive hepatosplenomegaly. Labs show normal RBC with elevated TLC (>40,000) and platelet counts. Peripheral smear reveals immature WBC with basophils called bone marrow appearance.
t(8:21) translocation (Option D): t(8:21) translocation is seen in the M2 subtype of AML (most common). Associated with chloroma. The smear reveals > 10% mature myeloid cells, not Auer rods.
